title: EDHEC Private Equity, VC & M&A — Final Exam 2023
notice: Derived study pack: questions are condensed and paraphrased from the 2023 EDHEC past paper; numerical answers and worked solutions are reproduced.

questions.prompt: Which statement about private equity is FALSE?

choices.text: There is a liquid secondary market for trading PE investments.
PE is sometimes accused of short-term measures that boost exit value at the expense of long-term prospects.
A company may use PE financing to repurchase shares and go private.
An entrepreneur can use business-angel networks to source seed capital.

questions.solution: PE interests are illiquid and trade only on a limited secondary market, usually through fund stakes or structured secondaries.

questions.prompt: Which PE strategy sees the highest euro amount invested in Europe every year?

choices.text: Buyout.
Growth equity.
Venture capital.
Rescue / turnaround.

questions.solution: Buyout is the largest PE segment by invested capital in Europe; VC is much smaller in euro terms.

questions.prompt: VC firms typically use staged financing in order to:

choices.text: Incentivize the entrepreneur to reach predefined milestones.
Acquire information about the founder's true ability, reducing informational asymmetries.
Keep the option to abandon low-return ventures and fund only good performers.
All of the above.

questions.solution: All three motives are standard: incentives, information acquisition and the abandonment option.

questions.prompt: The amount invested in a venture deal:

choices.text: Affects pre-money valuation.
Affects post-money valuation.
Affects both pre- and post-money valuation.
Does not affect valuation.

questions.solution: Post-money = pre-money + investment. The negotiated pre-money value is independent of the cheque size.

questions.prompt: A stock-options pool is 'fully diluted' when:

choices.text: Later rounds dilute the pool's ownership stake.
All options are exercised and converted into common shares.
Employees let options expire because they are worthless.
Grants exceed the issued share capital.

questions.solution: Fully diluted treats all options and convertibles as exercised/converted.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics represent an attractive LBO candidate?

choices.text: Irregular cash flow and substantial assets.
High capex requirements and a small asset base.
Predictable cash flow and substantial assets.
Substantial assets and insubstantial cash flow.

questions.solution: LBOs need stable cash flow to service debt and assets to collateralize it.

questions.prompt: All of the following are reasons why EBITDA matters in comparable-company analysis EXCEPT:

choices.text: It is a more accurate look at operating cash flow.
It is free from capital-structure differences.
It represents profit after all expenses have been netted out.
It is free from tax differences.

questions.solution: EBITDA is before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; it is not profit after all expenses.

questions.prompt: What happens to enterprise value if a company issues equity and uses the proceeds to repay debt?

choices.text: EV goes up.
EV remains the same.
EV goes down.
It depends.

questions.solution: Equity rises by the amount debt falls (cash is unchanged after the round-trip), so EV = equity + debt - cash is unchanged.

questions.prompt: In an LBO, which correctly ranks the capital structure from most senior to most junior?

choices.text: High-yield bonds, mezzanine, equity, bank debt.
Equity, mezzanine, high-yield bonds, bank debt.
Equity, high-yield bonds, mezzanine, bank debt.
Bank debt, mezzanine, high-yield bonds, equity.

questions.solution: Bank debt is senior secured; mezzanine is subordinated; high-yield bonds are typically unsecured/junior; equity is last.

questions.prompt: Which generally provides the highest valuation on a football-field graphic?

choices.text: DCF.
LBO.
Company comparables.
Transaction comparables.

questions.solution: Transaction comparables include a control premium and synergies, so they usually sit at the top of the football field.

questions.prompt: EBITDA is $200m, COGS $200m, sales $1,000m and net income $150m. What is the EBITDA margin?
questions.solution: EBITDA margin = 200 / 1,000 = 20%. COGS and net income are distractors.

questions.prompt: Offer price $20, fully diluted shares 100m, total debt $200m, cash $100m. What is the implied enterprise value ($m)?
questions.solution: Equity value = 20 × 100 = $2,000m. EV = equity + debt - cash = 2,000 + 200 - 100 = $2,100m.

questions.prompt: EBITDA $600m, capex $100m, interest $150m, increase in NWC $40m, D&A $200m, tax rate 40%. What is free cash flow ($m)?
XO invested $10m five years ago in 5m convertible preferred shares (3 common each). Its common position is 30% of equity. IPO price $10, 8% underwriting fee. What exit proceeds can XO expect ($m)?
questions.solution: XO's 15m common shares are 30% of 50m total. Market cap = 50m × $10 = $500m; after the 8% fee = $460m; XO gets 30% = $138m.

questions.prompt: Using the XO data above, what is the IRR on the investment?
What are the steps of capital allocation in a distribution waterfall?
questions.answer: 1) Return contributed capital to LPs. 2) Pay the preferred return/hurdle (about 8%). 3) GP catch-up until the GP has 20% of profits. 4) Split the remainder 80/20 between LPs and GP. 5) Clawback if the GP was overpaid.
questions.solution: The standard European waterfall is deal-by-deal or fund-wide: capital, hurdle, catch-up, 80/20 carry, then a clawback/true-up at the end.

questions.prompt: In seed investing, what are convertible notes and when/why are they used?
questions.answer: Short-term debt-like instruments that convert into preferred shares at the next priced round, usually with a discount (10-20%) and/or a valuation cap. They avoid pricing an immature startup, are fast and cheap, and give the investor downside protection and control rights. Typical maturity is 12-24 months.
questions.solution: Key points: no valuation at issuance, conversion at a discount/cap, maturity and interest, speed and standardisation, and the tension between founder and investor incentives if the next round is delayed.

questions.prompt: Growth-equity funds target firms with high capex and working-capital needs. What are the three main types of target firms?
questions.answer: Mature SMEs; late-stage VC-backed firms/startups; corporate spin-offs/carve-outs.
questions.solution: Growth equity sits between VC and buyout: minority stakes, proven business models, capital for scaling rather than survival.

questions.prompt: Explain rollover equity. Is it a positive or a negative sign?
questions.answer: Equity that key pre-buyout shareholders (management, sometimes the seller) reinvest into the post-buyout company instead of cashing out. It is generally positive: it aligns management with the PE owner and signals the seller's continued belief; it also reduces the PE equity cheque. It can be negative if the seller wanted a full exit or if the fit with the PE is poor.
questions.solution: Mention alignment, signalling and financing benefits; also mention the seller's liquidity preference and potential conflicts.

questions.prompt: When would a sell-side M&A advisor recommend a broad auction?
questions.answer: When maximizing competition and price is the priority: a broad auction reaches many strategic and financial buyers, limits any single buyer's bargaining power and helps the board meet its fiduciary duty. Costs: heavy preparation, confidentiality risk, business disruption and 'taint' if the auction fails.
questions.solution: Contrast with a targeted process: a broad auction maximizes price but is noisy; a targeted process protects confidentiality and is better when the buyer set is narrow.

questions.prompt: Epäkunnossa Partners considers two startups. Both need €2m and would exit at €20m after two years if successful. Häviäjä: 10% success probability; Voittaja: 30%. Each founder has €3m expected lifetime income. The fund does not observe the founders' beliefs and assumes 20% success for both. It offers €2m at an €8m post-money with a 10% annual dividend and a 1.3x liquidation preference.

parts.prompt: What is each startup's expected exit value under the founder's belief? Is it worth investing (scrap value 0)?
parts.answer: Häviäjä: 10% × €20m = €2m (indifferent, not worth it after any hurdle). Voittaja: 30% × €20m = €6m (worth it).
parts.solution: Expected exit value = probability × exit value: €2m vs €6m. Against a €2m investment, Häviäjä barely breaks even; Voittaja has a positive expected payoff.

parts.prompt: What ownership fraction and preferred terms does the offer imply? What is the conversion threshold?
parts.solution: Preferred terms: 1.3× liquidation preference (€2.6m) plus two years of 10% dividends (€0.4m) = €3.0m. The VC converts when 25% of exit exceeds €3m, i.e. above €12m.

parts.prompt: On success, what are the payoffs for the VC and the founders?
parts.answer: Exit €20m > €12m threshold, so the VC converts: VC = 25% × €20m = €5m; founders = €15m.
parts.solution: Because conversion beats the preference (€5m > €3m), the VC converts. Founders keep the residual €15m.

parts.prompt: Would each founder accept, given €3m lifetime income? Does the term sheet screen out the weaker startup?
parts.answer: Häviäjä: 10% × €15m = €1.5m < €3m → reject. Voittaja: 30% × €15m = €4.5m > €3m → accept. Yes, the contract screens out the low-quality startup.
parts.solution: The founder compares the expected payoff with the outside option (€3m). Only the high-type founder accepts, so the term sheet is a screening device.

questions.prompt: Æble PE Partners buys Eple Co. at 8x LTM EBITDA and exits after three years at the same 8x. 50% debt at 10% with a cash sweep. LTM revenue $100m, growing 20% for two years; EBITDA margin 40%, flat; capex and depreciation 20% of revenue; no change in NWC; no tax for three years.

parts.prompt: Compute revenue, EBITDA, entry EV and exit EV ($m).
parts.solution: Revenue grows 20%: 100, 120, 144, 172.8. EBITDA = 40% of revenue: 40, 48, 57.6, 69.12. EV = 8 × EBITDA: 320 entry, 552.96 exit.

parts.prompt: Compute free cash flow and debt for each year ($m).
parts.solution: CFADS = EBITDA - capex (20% of revenue), NWC change 0. Interest = 10% of opening debt. FCF = CFADS - interest. Debt falls by FCF each year (cash sweep).

parts.prompt: Compute the exit equity value, cash return, CCM and IRR. Would you invest?
parts.answer: Exit equity = 552.96 - 117.68 = $435.28m; entry equity = $160m; return = $275.28m; CCM = 2.72x; IRR = 39.6%; yes (above the ~20-25% LBO threshold).
parts.solution: Equity = EV - debt. CCM = 435.28/160 = 2.72x. IRR = 2.72^(1/3) - 1 = 39.6%. The deal clears the usual LBO hurdle.

parts.prompt: Decompose the return into EBITDA, multiple and net-debt effects.
parts.solution: EBITDA impact = ΔEBITDA × entry multiple. Multiple impact = (exit multiple - entry multiple) × exit EBITDA = 0. Net-debt impact = entry debt - exit debt. The three sum to the $275.28m return.
